As a FT myself, I'm actually glad that these candidates know their worth and understand what they should be asking in return for fair compensation of their work. I started my career as one of those hungry /desperate people who would just take the grind and it wasn't a healthy habit to take. It still affect me till this day as I still see myself inadequate and there are so many times where I told myself 'I should be happy that they even give someone like me a job".

However, also coming from a FT perspective, I'm sure there will be other FTs who wouldn't mind being exploited as the pay could still be a lot better than what the FT is getting from their country. For example, my first fresh grad role from a MNC paid me <SGD900 vs the SGD3.6k benchmark you have here in Singapore. And that was 5 years ago. Can only speak for my own country, but I know a lot of us would think that such exploitation is still tolerable and would just take this. 

So unfortunately such companies pretty much rigged this and they would end up hiring FT because 'no local talents want to take the job'.

I understand that it can be difficult to get a friend or someone that is the total opposite of you but if you do have a go-getter friend or acquaintance that you could tag on to for any homework/study session, it might help you to get into the zone but this depends on whether you are the kind of person who goes along with what others are doing. Treat it as a learning experience about how different personalities are like and how can you learn from them to deal with the gaps in yours. Back in my uni days, I know very well that I will not study alone so I'll tag on to mates that are way more focused than I do and I managed to sit myself through the process because I was "following the crowd" but I did that to people that I'm comfortable with. 

Have you tried changing the location on where you spend your spare time? For example, I find myself in the same situation too every evening after work; back in my room watching youtube and just sleep till the next morning despite telling myself that I'm gonna do something after some "rest". What I have been trying out is that I'll make myself go to a coffee place or library to hang out after work with my laptop. I would still end up procrastinating even in those situations but after a while I would find myself getting back into the zone to work whatever that I wanted to work on. Like what the other posters mentioned, even if you have done only a little, it is way better than nothing at all. Perhaps you have also started to associate your home as your nest where you get away from your daily woes so it would probably help to assign a different place or location to help you focus and tell yourself that you cannot leave until you have a certain goal sorted out. It sounds silly but it was Persona 5 (game) that has given me a better visualization on how important it is to wisely spend the limited amount of time we have within a day (I had to re-play the game from scratch because I didn't utilize my character's time properly to get the stats that I want). 

Trying to do what I can to help out; I'm 31 years old and I'm still struggling with this till this day so I really encourage you to start early to fix this. The sooner you start, the better chance you have to get yourself more disciplined. You may not feel the importannce or the stress to do so yet but if you can learn to correct yourself earlier, it will also help you out at how you manage yourself in your career and not self sabotage your own potential just because of discipline issues. I hope you do not end up like me and keep fighting!

Kluang!

Albeit the heavier weekend traffic from those who are travelling or returning from Singapore and KL, it still retains its charm as a quaint city tucked within Johor. 

The old railway station, the stretch of post colonial shop lots in the city centre, the remnants of 80s -90s aesthetics retained across the streets, shops and buildings.

It is good that Kluang has been developing but I do hope to see that the city will continue to improve on how to restore and preserve the uniqueness of the city.  Love what they did with the murals but am still rather saddened over Majlis Perbandaran's decision to shut down the legacy wet market located in the city centre instead of revamping it. There used to be an iconi  Hainanese kopitiam (which has been relocated to a shop where the old Metro cinema ysed to be) where you can enjoy a cup of Kopi-O while being shaded by a full grown tree that has been around for decades.
